items.body: Knowing the books in order makes it quick to find a passage, and it shows how the Bible is laid out: the Pentateuch, the historical books, the wisdom books and the prophets, then the Gospels and letters.

meta.technique: Seventy-three names is a long list, so chunk it by section: the Pentateuch, the historical books, the wisdom books, the prophets, then the New Testament. items.title: Books of the Bible (66-book Protestant canon)
items.subtitle: 66 items · scripture
items.body: Knowing the books in order makes it quick to find a passage, and it shows how the Bible is laid out: law, history, poetry, prophets, then the Gospels and letters. Families have learned this list by heart for generations, often as a song.

meta.technique: Sixty-six names is a long list, so chunk it by section. The sections are the meaningful units: five books of Law, twelve of History, five of Poetry and wisdom, five Major prophets, twelve Minor prophets, then the New Testament. Long sections are split into groups of about five. A tune helps too: sing each section to a melody you already know, and the rhythm carries the order.

meta.hook: Genesis means 'origin' in Greek: the book of beginnings.
Exodus means 'the way out': the road out of Egypt.
Deuteronomy means 'second law' in Greek: the law told a second time.
Joshua leads the people into the promised land, so the history books start here.

items.title: The ten brightest stars in the night sky
items.subtitle: 10 items · science
items.body: These ten stars are the easiest to find on a clear night and anchor the constellations around them. Learn them and the sky becomes a map you can read, season by season.

meta.technique: Order by brightness is the hard part, so chunk: the big three (Sirius, Canopus, Alpha Centauri), then the next four, then the last three. Hang each star on its constellation, and the constellation on a picture: two dogs (Sirius, Procyon), a hunter with a blue foot and a red shoulder (Rigel, Betelgeuse). Then go outside: finding Sirius below Orion's belt once is worth ten flashcards.

items.title: The ten main cloud types
items.subtitle: 10 items · science
items.body: Every cloud in the sky belongs to one of ten families, and their names are built from just four Latin words. Learn the ten and a glance upward tells you something about the weather on the way.

meta.technique: Build from the parts first: cirrus (curl of hair, high and icy), cumulus (heap), stratus (spread out, a layer) and nimbus (rain cloud), plus alto for the middle level. Then each name is a small sum you can work out, which is far easier than ten separate facts. Chunk by level (three high, three middle, four low), and pair each name with a quick sketch: picture plus words is dual coding. Best of all, step outside and name the clouds you see.

items.subtitle: abbr: Ci · level: High · height: About 5-13 km (16,500-45,000 ft) · looks: Thin white wisps, strands or hooks of ice cry

meta.name: Cirrus
meta.looks: Thin white wisps, strands or hooks of ice crystals, like brush strokes across the sky.
meta.hook: Latin cirrus means a curl or lock of hair: picture the sky with wispy white hair.

items.title: Cirrocumulus

meta.name: Cirrocumulus
meta.looks: Tiny white grains or ripples in rows, with no shading; each bit looks smaller than your little finger held at arm's length.
meta.hook: Cirro (hair-high) + cumulus (heap): tiny heaps up where the cirrus lives, like fish scales.

items.title: Cirrostratus

meta.name: Cirrostratus
meta.looks: A thin, milky veil over much of the sky that often makes a ring of light (a halo) around the Sun or Moon.
meta.hook: Cirro + stratus (spread out): a thin icy sheet spread high up, wearing a halo.

meta.name: Altocumulus
meta.looks: White or gray patches, rolls or rows with some shading; each piece about one to three fingers wide at arm's length.
meta.hook: Alto (from Latin altus, high) + cumulus: heaps in the middle of the sky, like a flock of sheep.

items.title: Altostratus
items.subtitle: abbr: As · level: Middle · height: About 2-7 km (6,500-23,000 ft) · looks: A gray or bluish sheet; the Sun shows dimly,

meta.name: Altostratus
meta.looks: A gray or bluish sheet; the Sun shows dimly, as if through frosted glass, with no halo.
meta.hook: Alto + stratus: a middle-level sheet that turns the Sun into a dim, blurry coin.

items.title: Nimbostratus
items.subtitle: abbr: Ns · level: Middle · height: About 2-7 km (6,500-23,000 ft) · looks: A thick, dark gray layer that hides the Sun a

meta.name: Nimbostratus
meta.looks: A thick, dark gray layer that hides the Sun and brings steady rain or snow.
meta.hook: Latin nimbus means rain cloud: a rain-sheet that settles in for the whole day.

items.title: Stratocumulus
items.subtitle: abbr: Sc · level: Low · height: Surface to about 2 km (6,500 ft) · looks: Low gray or white lumps and rolls with darker

meta.name: Stratocumulus
meta.looks: Low gray or white lumps and rolls with darker parts, each wider than three fingers at arm's length, often with gaps of blue.
meta.hook: Strato + cumulus: lumpy heaps spread into a low blanket, like a quilt with patches.

items.title: Stratus

meta.name: Stratus
meta.looks: A flat, even gray layer, like fog that has lifted off the ground; it may bring drizzle.
meta.hook: Stratus (spread out): a flat gray lid on the sky. Fog is stratus at ground level.

items.title: Cumulus
items.subtitle: abbr: Cu · level: Low · height: Surface to about 2 km (6,500 ft) · looks: Puffy, separate heaps with flat bases and brig

meta.name: Cumulus
meta.looks: Puffy, separate heaps with flat bases and bright, rounded tops, like cotton balls or cauliflower.
meta.hook: Latin cumulus means heap (as in "accumulate"): fair-weather heaps of cotton.

items.title: Cumulonimbus
items.subtitle: abbr: Cb · level: Low · height: Surface to about 2 km (6,500 ft) · looks: A huge, towering storm cloud, often with a fla

meta.name: Cumulonimbus
meta.looks: A huge, towering storm cloud, often with a flat anvil-shaped top, bringing thunder, lightning, heavy showers and sometimes hail.
meta.hook: Cumulus + nimbus: a heap that grew into a rain-and-thunder tower.

items.title: Common thinking traps (cognitive biases)
items.subtitle: 12 items · science
items.body: Everyone's mind takes shortcuts, and most of the time they serve us well. These twelve are the places where the shortcuts lead us wrong in predictable ways. Knowing their names makes them easier to catch, in yourself first.

meta.technique: Encode each bias with your own example: after reading the everyday one, think of a time it happened to you and say it out loud. A personal story is far stickier than a definition. Chunk them by what they bend (judging numbers, looking ahead and back, beliefs and choices, judging people). Then practice retrieval in real life: name a bias when you see it in an ad or a story.

meta.example: After a news story about a plane crash, flying feels riskier than driving, though per mile driving is far more dangerous.

meta.means: Believing good things are more likely, and bad things less likely, to happen to you than to other people.
meta.example: Expecting your old car will keep running fine, though you know cars that age often break down.

meta.means: Noticing, believing and remembering the facts that fit what you already think, and passing over the ones that don't.

items.title: The 27 amendments to the U.S. Constitution
items.subtitle: 27 items · civics
items.body: The amendments are the changes and additions the country has made to its Constitution since 1787. Knowing them by number makes news, history and civics lessons easier to follow, since people often name a right by its amendment.

meta.technique: Chunk by era. The ten amendments of the Bill of Rights come first, learned five at a time. Then come the early fixes (11 and 12), the three Reconstruction amendments after the Civil War (13, 14 and 15), the four of the Progressive Era (16 to 19), and the rest in small groups. Use a number-shape or number-rhyme peg for each: one is a lone speaker at a microphone, three is a crowded house, five is a hand raised to say no. items.title: The seven articles of the U.S. Constitution
items.subtitle: 7 items · civics
items.body: The Constitution has only seven articles, and each has one job. Once you know which article does what, the whole document has a map: the three branches first, then the states, then how to change it, how it stands above other laws, and how it came into force.

meta.technique: Seven things fit in a short list, so learn all seven as one chunk. A first-letter sentence helps hold the order: Lively Eagles Jump Over Steep Stony Ridges, for Legislative, Executive, Judicial, the States, Amendments (changing it), Supreme law, Ratification. Then build pictures on a memory palace route: a busy hall of lawmakers at the front door, a desk with a presidential seal in the hall, a judge's gavel on the stairs, fifty state flags in the kitchen, a pencil and eraser in the dining room, a crown on the top shelf, and nine signatures on the back door. Recall it by walking the route, and come back on day 1, 3, 7 and 21.

items.title: The dwarf planets, in order from the Sun
items.subtitle: 5 items · science
items.body: In 2006 astronomers created a new group, the dwarf planets, for round worlds that orbit the Sun but have not cleared their path of other objects. Pluto is the most famous; one sits in the asteroid belt and the rest are far beyond Neptune.

meta.technique: Five fits in one chunk. Make a first-letter sentence for the order (C, P, H, M, E), for example "Curious Penguins Hike Many Evenings," or better, one of your own. items.title: Element symbols that come from old names
items.subtitle: 11 items · science
items.body: Most element symbols match their English names: O for oxygen, C for carbon. A few do not, because they come from the old Latin names that chemists used when the symbols were set in the 1800s. These eleven trip people up, so they are worth learning on their own.

meta.technique: These are pairs (symbol and name) that don't look alike, which is exactly where a mnemonic earns its keep. Make each pair into one vivid picture that holds both, like the hooks below, then test yourself from both sides: symbol to name and name to symbol. Saying the old name out loud ("aurum") is the bridge between the two.

items.title: Elements 1-18: the first three rows of the periodic table
items.subtitle: 18 items · science
items.body: The first eighteen elements are the ones you meet most: the air you breathe, the water you drink, the salt on the table and the sand on the beach. Learn these and the shape of the whole periodic table starts to make sense.

meta.technique: Eighteen is too many to hold at once, so take it a row at a time: row 1 has two elements, rows 2 and 3 have eight each, and the engine splits each row into two chunks of four. Picture each row as a shelf in your kitchen, and put a vivid object for each element on it, left to right (a balloon for helium, a battery for lithium, a diamond for carbon). Say the symbols out loud as you walk the shelf, then look away and rebuild it.

items.title: The four eons of Earth's history
items.subtitle: 4 items · science
items.body: Earth is about 4.5 billion years old, and geologists split that long story into four huge chapters called eons. Knowing them gives you a frame for everything else: fossils, mountains, and how short human history is.

meta.technique: Four items fit in working memory at once, so learn them as one chunk. The names tell the story if you know their Greek roots: Hades (fiery start), archaios (ancient), proteros + zoe (earlier life), phaneros + zoe (visible life). Make it a four-panel comic: a fiery ball, a rock with a speck of life, green slime and bubbles of oxygen, then a busy sea of creatures.

meta.name: Hadean

items.title: The eras of geologic time
items.subtitle: 10 items · science
items.body: Eras are the second level of the time scale. Most people know the last three (Paleozoic, Mesozoic, Cenozoic); the seven older ones fill in the long, quiet stretch when life was small.

meta.technique: The names follow one pattern, so learn the pattern, not ten words: Eo (dawn), Paleo (old), Meso (middle), Neo (new), attached to the eon's name. The Archean gets all four, the Proterozoic gets three (no Eo), and the Phanerozoic's three use -zoic alone. Chunk by eon, and anchor the last three with pictures: a trilobite, a dinosaur, a mammoth.

meta.name: Eoarchean
meta.hook: Eo- means dawn: the dawn of the Archean, with the oldest known rocks.

meta.name: Paleoarchean
meta.hook: Paleo- means old. Stromatolites, mounds built by microbes, are among the oldest signs of life.

meta.name: Mesoarchean
meta.hook: Meso- means middle.

meta.name: Neoarchean
meta.hook: Neo- means new: the last era of the Archean.

meta.name: Paleoproterozoic
meta.hook: Old Proterozoic: oxygen begins to build up in the air.

meta.name: Mesoproterozoic
meta.hook: Middle Proterozoic.

meta.name: Neoproterozoic
meta.hook: New Proterozoic: "snowball Earth" ice ages and the first many-celled animals.

meta.name: Paleozoic
meta.hook: Paleozoic means "old life": trilobites, fish, the first forests.

meta.name: Mesozoic
meta.hook: Mesozoic means "middle life": the age of dinosaurs.

meta.name: Cenozoic
meta.hook: Cenozoic means "new life": the age of mammals, including us.

items.title: The periods of the last 539 million years
items.subtitle: 12 items · science
items.body: These twelve periods are the story of complex life, from the first animals with shells to today. They are the names you see in museums, on fossil labels and in dinosaur books.

meta.technique: Use a first-letter sentence for the order: "Cows Often Sit Down Calmly; Perhaps To Just Chew Peacefully, Not Quickly." Then chunk by era: six Paleozoic periods (old life), three Mesozoic (dinosaurs), three Cenozoic (mammals). Give each period one picture from the 'what lived' column and place them along a long hallway, oldest by the front door. Learn the order first; add the start dates once the order is solid.

items.title: The Gettysburg Address
items.subtitle: 20 items · history
items.body: Abraham Lincoln gave this short speech on November 19, 1863, at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, four and a half months after the battle there. It takes about two minutes to say and is one of the most famous speeches in American history, which makes it a classic piece of memory work.

meta.technique: Narrate it first: read it aloud and say what each paragraph does. The first looks back to 1776, the second looks at the battlefield, and the third looks ahead. Those three are your big chunks. Inside each, learn three or four phrases at a time and recite with the page covered. Lincoln built the speech on patterns that help memory: three in a row (dedicate, consecrate, hallow; of the people, by the people, for the people) and pairs (living and dead; say here, did here). Picture each phrase on a walk across the field, and come back on day 1, 3, 7 and 21.

items.title: The Greek alphabet
items.subtitle: 24 items · language
items.body: The Greek letters turn up all over: in math (π, Σ, θ), science (α, β and γ rays, μ for micro), college names and the roots of thousands of English words. The alphabet itself is named for its first two letters.

meta.technique: Many letters look like ours (A, B, E, Z, I, K, M, N, O, T), so start by sorting: the look-alikes, the false friends that look like ours but sound different (H is the vowel eta, P is r, X is ch), and the new shapes (Γ, Δ, Θ, Λ, Ξ, Π, Σ, Φ, Ψ, Ω). Then learn the order in chunks of five or so, saying the names in rhythm as a chant. Write each letter by hand as you say it: the motion, the picture and the sound together make a strong memory.

items.title: Major organs of the human body and what they do
items.subtitle: 16 items · science
items.body: Knowing where your organs are and what each one does makes sense of how food, air and blood move through you. It is the first map every doctor, nurse and biology student learns.

meta.technique: Your own body is a ready-made memory palace. Walk it from top to bottom: brain, then the thyroid and esophagus in the neck, the heart and lungs in the chest, the five organs of the upper belly, the kidneys at the back, the intestines and bladder low down, and the skin wrapped around it all. Touch each spot as you name it and say its job in a few words. Chunking by region keeps each stop to five or fewer.

items.title: Math formulas, level 2: algebra and geometry
items.subtitle: 12 items · math
items.body: These are the workhorse formulas of algebra and geometry classes: right triangles, lines on a graph, the quadratic formula, and the volumes of round solids.

meta.technique: Tie each formula to the one it grows from. The distance formula is the Pythagorean theorem on a graph. Slope is rise over run, and the two line equations are slope rearranged. The cone is one third of a cylinder with the same base and height. Learn the parents first, then derive the children once by hand: working it out is the strongest way to encode it. Sing the quadratic formula to a tune you know.

items.body: Perimeter, area and volume come up everywhere: painting a wall, fencing a garden, filling a fish tank. Each formula is short, and each one makes sense once you see where it comes from.

meta.technique: Don't memorize these as strings of letters; rebuild them from a picture. Area of a rectangle is rows times columns of unit squares (l x w). items.title: Exact metric conversions

items.body: When a recipe, a science lab or a trip abroad switches between inches and centimeters or pounds and kilograms, these are the numbers behind every conversion chart. Most of them grow out of just two: the inch (2.54 cm) and the pound (0.45359237 kg).

meta.technique: Learn the two roots first, the inch and the pound, and derive the rest: a foot is 12 inches, so 12 x 2.54 = 30.48 cm. Working it out once is a strong encoding step, and it turns ten facts into two facts plus reasoning. Then use rounded versions for everyday sense (a mile is about 1.6 km, a kilogram about 2.2 pounds) and the exact ones when it matters. Chunk as length, weight, volume, temperature.

items.title: Metric prefixes, from tera to pico
items.subtitle: 12 items · math
items.body: Every metric unit uses the same set of prefixes, so learning these twelve unlocks meters, grams, liters, watts and bytes all at once. Each step is a power of ten, which is what makes the metric system easy to convert.

meta.technique: Build from first principles: each prefix means 'times ten to some power.' From kilo down to milli the steps go one power of ten at a time (kilo, hecto, deka, base, deci, centi, milli: "Kind Hippos Dance Barefoot During Chilly Mornings"), and outside that range they jump three powers at a time (mega, giga, tera; micro, nano, pico). Chunk them that way: the big jumps, the small steps, the tiny jumps.

items.title: The phases of the Moon, in order
items.subtitle: 8 items · science
items.body: The Moon does not change shape. Half of it is always lit by the Sun, and as it circles Earth we see more or less of that lit half. Learn the eight names and you can tell, just by looking, whether the Moon is growing or shrinking and when it will be full.

meta.technique: Start from the idea, not the words: a ball lit from one side, seen from different angles. Try it with a lamp and an orange. Then learn two word pairs: waxing means growing, waning means shrinking; crescent is less than half, gibbous is more than half. The eight names now build themselves in two chunks of four. In the Northern Hemisphere, D-O-C helps: a growing Moon is lit on the right like a D, full is an O, and a shrinking Moon is lit on the left like a C.

items.title: The NATO phonetic alphabet
items.subtitle: 26 items · everyday
items.body: When a letter is said over a phone or a radio, B, D, P and V can sound the same. The phonetic alphabet gives each letter a word that can't be mistaken. It is handy for spelling a name or a booking code, and it is used every day by pilots, sailors and emergency services.

meta.technique: Twenty-six words is about five chunks of five. Most words start with their own letter, so the letter is the cue and the word is the picture: picture each one as you say it (a bravo crowd cheering, a foxtrot dancer, a golf ball, a hotel, a kilo of flour, a lime from Lima). Link the words of a chunk into a short story: Alfa and Bravo watch Charlie fish in the Delta, and hear an Echo. Spell your own name out loud with it every day, then try street signs and license plates. Come back on day 1, 3, 7 and 21.

items.title: The Preamble to the Constitution
items.subtitle: 9 items · civics
items.body: The Preamble is the opening sentence of the Constitution. It says who is acting (we the people), why (six goals), and what they are doing (making a Constitution). It is short enough to learn in a week and is a classic first piece of memory work.

meta.technique: Narrate it first: say it aloud, then say in your own words what each goal means. Then chunk it. The six goals in the middle are the hard part, so give them a first-letter chain, U J T D W L (Union, Justice, Tranquility, defence, Welfare, Liberty), and a picture each: a knot tying states together, a balance scale, a sleeping cat, a shield, a full dinner table, a torch. items.title: Roman numerals
items.subtitle: 13 items · math
items.body: Roman numerals still turn up on clocks, in book chapters, after kings' and queens' names, on cornerstones and in the credits of old films. Thirteen symbols are all you need to read and write them.

meta.technique: Learn the seven letters first as one chunk, with a first-letter sentence for the order: I Value Xylophones Like Cows Dig Milk (1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1,000). Notice the pattern: each step is times 5, then times 2 (1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1,000). Then learn the six pairs, which follow one rule: a smaller letter before a bigger one is subtracted, and only I, X and C are used that way, each before the next two letters up (IV and IX, XL and XC, CD and CM). To write a number, take the biggest symbol that fits, write it, subtract, and repeat: 2026 is M M (2,000), X X (20), V I (6), so MMXXVI. Practice on dates and clock faces, and come back on day 1, 3, 7 and 21.

items.title: Famous laws of science
items.subtitle: 22 items · science
items.body: A scientific law is a short statement of something nature always does, tested again and again. These are the ones that turn up in every physics and chemistry class, and knowing who found them, and when, ties science to history.

meta.technique: Encode the meaning before the name: for each law, picture the everyday scene in the hook and say the law in your own words (narration). Then hang it on a timeline, chunked by century, so the people line up in order: Archimedes alone in the ancient world, then Kepler, Boyle, Hooke and Newton in the 1600s, and so on. Retrieve it by explaining one law a day to someone else.

meta.note: Mikhail Lomonosov showed the same idea decades earlier, but his work was less known. Lavoisier stated it in his 1789 textbook.

meta.says: The current through a wire equals the voltage across it divided by its resistance (I = V / R).

items.title: Law of conservation of energy (first law of thermodynamics)
items.subtitle: who: Hermann von Helmholtz · year: 1847 · says: Energy is never created or destroyed; it only changes from one form to a

meta.law: Law of conservation of energy (first law of thermodynamics)
meta.says: Energy is never created or destroyed; it only changes from one form to another.
meta.note: Built on work by Julius Robert von Mayer (1842) and James Prescott Joule (1840s); Rudolf Clausius wrote it as the first law of thermodynamics in 1850.

meta.says: Heat flows on its own from hot to cold, never from cold to hot; some energy always spreads out as unusable heat.
meta.hook: A hot cup of cocoa always cools to room temperature; it never heats itself up.
meta.note: Lord Kelvin gave another form of it in 1851, building on Sadi Carnot (1824).

meta.hook: Mendel worked it out by growing and counting thousands of pea plants.
meta.note: Presented in 1865 and published in 1866; mostly overlooked until 1900.

meta.note: Georges Lemaître proposed it in 1927; Hubble published the observations in 1929. The International Astronomical Union recommended the name Hubble-Lemaître law in 2018.

items.title: U.S. customary units: how many in one?
items.subtitle: 15 items · everyday
items.body: Recipes, road signs, lumber and gas pumps in the United States all use these units. Knowing how they nest inside each other lets you double a recipe, measure a room or read a map without reaching for a calculator.

meta.technique: Learn each family as one chain, since the units nest: teaspoon, tablespoon, fluid ounce, cup, pint, quart, gallon (3, 2, 8, 2, 2, 4). Draw it once as nesting boxes, a big G with four Qs inside, two Ps in each Q and two Cs in each P: picture plus words. Then length (12, 3, 5,280), weight (16, 2,000) and area (43,560, 640). Say each fact as a sentence, "one gallon is four quarts," and quiz yourself both ways.

A yardstick is three rulers end to end.

1,760 is 5,280 divided by 3.

items.title: Presidents of the United States, in order

items.body: Knowing the presidents in order gives American history a backbone. Each name becomes a hook to hang events on: wars, inventions, new states. It is a classic memory-work list, and it is long enough to show why chunking and spaced review matter.

meta.technique: Chunk first. Forty-seven names is far more than the four or so things the mind holds at once, so the list is split by era into groups of four to six. Learn one group, recall it with the book closed, then add the next. Old groups come back on day 1, 3, 7 and 21. For a stronger hook, walk a memory palace: Washington washing the front door, Adams with an apple in his throat on the mat, and so on, one picture per stop.

items.title: Major wars in U.S. history, 1754 to 1991

items.body: Wars are turning points in a nation's story, and their dates are anchors for everything around them: inventions, presidents, new states. This list gives only the dates and who was on each side, so the rest of history has something to hang on.

meta.technique: Chunk by century. The 1700s (two wars, both about who would rule North America), the 1800s (four), and the 1900s (five). Learn one century at a time, then recall the order before the dates. A number hook makes the years stick: 1812 is in the war's own name, and the Civil War's 1861 to 1865 starts with Lincoln's inauguration year. Tie each war to a picture in a memory palace, and come back on day 1, 3, 7 and 21.

items.body: A few wars show up again and again in history books, because they changed who ruled, where borders ran and how people lived afterward. Knowing their dates and sides gives the long story of the world a set of fixed points, from ancient Greece to the twentieth century.

meta.technique: Chunk by age: the ancient world (five wars, all BC), the Middle Ages (three), the early modern era (three), the 1800s (three) and the 1900s (six). Learn one age at a time and put the wars in order before learning the dates. For BC dates, remember that the numbers count down toward AD 1: the Greco-Persian Wars (499 BC) came before the Punic Wars (264 BC).
